The same trait in different populations

Source: vignettes/articles/same-trait-across-groups.Rmd
same-trait-across-groups.Rmd

中文版

Is growth in herd nls genetically the same trait as growth in herd bfs? If the genetic correlation between the two is high (say above 0.8), the best animals are the same in both herds; a lower value means re-ranking - genotype × environment interaction. The trait in each population is treated as a separate trait in a two-trait model.

Data: one column per population

cv_scenarios(scenarios = "mt_bt") builds the data directly: for every trait, one data set with a column per group level, keeping the fixed effects:

library(asreml)
library(mintyr)
library(mintyrasr)

sc <- cv_scenarios(pheno, cols = c("adg", "bf"), id = "id", group = "test_herd",
                   v = 5, repeats = 5, seed = 2026, scenarios = "mt_bt", out_type = "df")
sc$mt_bt$param                            # name (trait) | data
head(sc$mt_bt$param$data[[1]])            # id, test_herd, hhys, ..., nls, bfs

nls holds adg for animals in herd nls and is NA elsewhere; the same for bfs. (mintyr::r2p_nest() gives the same columns but keeps only the ID, so the fixed effects would have to be joined back.)

Genetic correlation between populations 

res <- asr_gblup(sc$mt_bt$param, ginv = ginv, traits = c("nls", "bfs"),
                 fixed = ~ hhys, residual_cov = "diag", rp = FALSE,
                 genetic_cov = "corgh", inbreeding = inbreeding)
res$param[, .(name, h2_nls, h2_bfs, rg, rg_se, rg_p, boundary, status)]
  • h2_nls, h2_bfs: heritability of the trait in each population.
  • rg: genetic correlation between the populations. With genetic_cov = "corgh" it is a parameter of the model and its SE comes directly; "us" gives the same value through Cova / √(Va,1 Va,2).
  • rg_p: LRT of rg = 0. The more interesting question is usually whether rg is below 1: compare the model with a correlation fixed close to 1 in asreml() (a boundary test).

Why there is no phenotypic correlation here

A phenotypic correlation needs both traits measured on the same individual. An animal is tested in one herd only, so its residuals in the two herds can never be observed together: the residual covariance is not estimable and is left out (residual_cov = "diag"), and rp - which needs it - is not defined (rp = FALSE). asr_scenarios(scenarios = "mt_bt") sets both for you.

Only if the same animals have records in both populations (e.g. the same animals tested in two environments) can you use residual_cov = "us" and rp = TRUE.

What the data must allow

rg between populations is estimated only from animals that are related across the populations: common sires, related dams, genomic relationships. With weak ties the likelihood is flat:

  • with us, the covariance stays near 0 and ASReml reports it as restrained; the LRT then has df = 0 and mintyrasr gives rg_p = NA with a log entry;
  • with corgh, the correlation runs to the boundary (±1) without SE; it is listed in boundary and in res$log.

Check before interpreting: the number of sires with progeny in both populations, or the mean genomic relationship between them, e.g. mean(G[ids_nls, ids_bfs]).

More than two populations

  • Run each pair of populations (one data set per pair), or
  • use the compound-symmetry model in one single-trait analysis: random = ~ vm(id, ginv):test_herd gives rB_test_herd, one common genetic correlation between all populations (see Beyond the animal model); or
  • factor-analytic models (fa()) in asreml() for many environments.

Prediction across populations

asr_scenarios(sc, ginv, scenarios = "mt_bt") cross-validates the model: the animals of one population are predicted from the records of both, using the genetic correlation. Compare it with st_sp (own population only) and st_mp (populations pooled as one trait).
